# **AI agents for design systems:**  **What I want to build this year**

## Design systems need to work smarter, not harder. With AI shifting what one designer is expected to do, this is how I plan to scale up without burning out.

[![Lindsey Norberg](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/1*99ijNlOzk8BVTHz7Ba7vbw.jpeg)](https://medium.com/@lindseynorberg?source=post_page---byline--3fb3057d1c0d---------------------------------------)

I’ve spent the last decade working on design systems. In that time, it has become increasingly clear that the role of the designer is evolving. The work is speeding up, teams are getting leaner, and **AI is quietly resetting expectations for what one person should be able to handle**. Design systems need to be more efficient than ever. This is how I plan to scale up without burning out.

We are still needed. But we are needed differently.

So this year, I’m shifting how I work.

Not by trying to do more, but by exploring how AI agents can carry part of the load.

## **Why AI agents?**

AI agents are not just tools. **They are workflows you design.**

Each one uses a large language model, a set of connected tools, and structured instructions to carry out a task on your behalf. If you work in design systems, you already think this way. You define structure. You write logic. You standardize patterns and behavior.

The skillset maps perfectly.

The only difference is the output is not a component or Figma library. It’s a task that runs without you having to do it manually.

**I’m not doing this just to save time. I’m doing it to stay strategic**, stay useful, and stay aligned with how the role is evolving.

## **Why design systems are a great place to start**

Design systems are essential, but fragile. They depend on upkeep, alignment, and adoption. And the workflows behind them are often messy, slow, or invisible.

This is exactly where AI has the potential to help. Not by generating components or visuals, but by supporting the behind-the-scenes work that keeps a system usable and trusted. From automating audits to syncing tokens and surfacing usage patterns, **AI agents can reduce the manual load** and make operations more scalable without sacrificing consistency.

Here are the common breakdowns I keep seeing:

- Outdated components still in use
- Contributions made without review or documentation
- Tokens falling out of sync across design and code
- Updates that never get shared with dev teams
- QA and accessibility reviews happening too late
- No visibility into real usage patterns

These are not just annoying. They chip away at trust in the system. And they are exactly the kind of repeatable tasks that AI can help with.

## **AI agents I plan to explore this year**

These are real, tactical ideas I’m actively mapping and prioritizing. Each one supports a specific part of the design system lifecycle.

**My goal is to speed up the parts of my workflow that slow me down**, so I can handle the responsibilities of multiple designers without burning out.

AI agents are not about doing more. They are about doing the right work faster, with less friction. They take care of the repetitive tasks and protect time for the parts of design that still need human judgment.

1. **Component Governance Agent**

Flags outdated, duplicate, or inconsistent components in Figma. Sends a cleanup report with suggested actions.
2. **Figma Audit Agent**

Acts as a design reviewer. Scans files for spacing, token use, and hierarchy before handoff. Outputs a visual checklist.
3. **Token Sync Agent**

Monitors token alignment between Figma and the codebase. Flags mismatches and suggests updates.
4. **Release Note Generator**

Summarizes component updates with clear language and visuals. Helps keep product and dev teams in the loop.
5. **Contribution Flow Assistant**

Guides contributors through proposing new patterns. Checks for redundancy. Generates a draft spec or documentation entry.
6. **Pattern Usage Explorer**

Analyzes adoption across teams and files. Highlights unused patterns or potential deprecations.
7. **Design QA Reviewer**

Checks for accessibility, design system violations, and inconsistent usage before dev handoff.

## No engineering background required

These agents do not need to be coded from scratch.

Designers at any skill level can start experimenting with tools like Replit, n8n, and GPT-based workflows. These platforms make it easy to prototype agents using the same logic we already apply to user flows and task mapping.

I am starting by identifying the right workflows, writing prompt scaffolding, and testing how agents can reduce cognitive load. Even early sketching has helped clarify what is worth automating and what still needs a human eye.

## Final thoughts

Design systems create consistency, but without the right workflows, they add overhead that most teams cannot sustain. **AI is not going to replace us, but it is already reshaping how we spend our time**. Designers who understand systems thinking, process design, and collaboration are in the best position to lead that shift. **We do not need to wait for perfect tools. We can start building the ones that support how we already work**.

If you could design an AI agent to support your workflow, what would it do? And if you are already experimenting with one, I would love to hear how it is going.
